Definition: % of identified CVEs remediated within the defined SLA per severity tier across the Linux server estate.
Level 1 - Ad Hoc: No vulnerability scanning. CVEs unknown. Patching done only in response to breaches.
Level 2 - Developing: Ad hoc scanning. CVEs identified but remediation unstructured. Critical CVEs take more than 30 days to fix.
Level 3 - Defined: Scanning automated. SLAs defined (Critical 14 days, High 30 days). Tracked but inconsistently met.
Level 4 - Managed: SLAs consistently met. Exception process exists. Vulnerability aging tracked and reported monthly.
Level 5 - Optimized: Critical CVEs remediated within 72 hours. Fully automated scan-to-patch pipeline. Zero unmitigated criticals.

Definition: % of Linux servers running a kernel version within the vendor-supported lifecycle such as RHEL, Ubuntu LTS, or SUSE.
Level 1 - Ad Hoc: Kernel versions not tracked. Multiple EOL kernels in production.
Level 2 - Developing: Kernel inventory exists but more than 20% on unsupported versions. No upgrade roadmap.
Level 3 - Defined: Inventory maintained. Upgrade plan in place. Between 5-20% on unsupported kernels.
Level 4 - Managed: Below 5% on unsupported kernels. Lifecycle tracked per distro. Kernel upgrade process defined.
Level 5 - Optimized: 100% on supported kernels. Automated lifecycle tracking. Kernel upgrades integrated in patch pipeline.

Definition: Adherence to the defined patching schedule per Linux distribution, measured as % of servers patched on time.
Level 1 - Ad Hoc: No patching schedule. Servers patched only after security incidents.
Level 2 - Developing: Patching schedule exists but less than 60% of servers patched on time. Manual process.
Level 3 - Defined: Between 60-85% of servers patched per schedule. Yum or APT automation partially deployed.
Level 4 - Managed: Between 85-95% of servers patched per schedule. Automated with Ansible, Satellite, or Landscape.
Level 5 - Optimized: More than 95% on-time compliance. Fully automated per distro. Staged rollout with health checks.

Definition: % of CIS Benchmark controls for the relevant Linux distribution passing across the managed estate, assessed via automated tooling such as OpenSCAP, Tenable, or Qualys.
Level 1 - Ad Hoc: No hardening baseline. Default OS configurations in production.
Level 2 - Developing: Some hardening applied manually. No formal benchmark. Score below 50%.
Level 3 - Defined: CIS benchmark adopted. Automated scanning in place. Score between 50-75%.
Level 4 - Managed: Score between 75-90%. Exceptions documented with risk acceptance. Integrated in build pipeline.
Level 5 - Optimized: Score above 90%. Benchmark enforced in golden image. Continuous drift monitoring.

Definition: % of Linux servers with SELinux on RHEL or AppArmor on Ubuntu running in Enforcing mode rather than Permissive or Disabled.
Level 1 - Ad Hoc: SELinux or AppArmor disabled on most systems. Security modules bypassed.
Level 2 - Developing: Modules installed but running in Permissive mode on most systems. Not enforced.
Level 3 - Defined: Enforcing mode on more than 60% of servers. Exceptions tracked. Policies periodically reviewed.
Level 4 - Managed: Enforcing mode on more than 90% of servers. Custom policies where needed. Alerts on violations.
Level 5 - Optimized: 100% enforcement. Custom policies managed as code. Automated violation detection and response.

Definition: Adherence to SSH security best practices including root login disabled, key-based auth enforced, idle timeout set, protocol version 2 only, and regular key rotation.
Level 1 - Ad Hoc: Root SSH login enabled. Password authentication allowed. No key rotation policy.
Level 2 - Developing: Some controls applied such as no root login but key rotation and idle timeout not enforced.
Level 3 - Defined: Core SSH controls enforced via configuration management. Key rotation process defined.
Level 4 - Managed: More than 90% of servers fully compliant with SSH policy. Automated compliance checks.
Level 5 - Optimized: 100% SSH policy compliance. SSH keys managed via PAM or vault. Auto-rotation. Full access audit trail.

Definition: % of Linux servers with auditd configured and forwarding logs to a centralised SIEM, covering key events such as auth, privilege escalation, file access, and network connections.
Level 1 - Ad Hoc: auditd not deployed. No central log collection from Linux systems.
Level 2 - Developing: auditd installed on some servers. Logs stored locally only. Not centralised.
Level 3 - Defined: auditd deployed on more than 70% of servers. Logs forwarded to central syslog or SIEM.
Level 4 - Managed: More than 95% coverage. Audit rules tuned to capture key security events. Alerts configured.
Level 5 - Optimized: 100% coverage with enriched audit rules. SIEM correlated. Automated anomaly detection.

Definition: % of Linux servers authenticating users via a centralised identity provider such as Active Directory via SSSD, FreeIPA, or LDAP rather than local accounts.
Level 1 - Ad Hoc: All authentication via local accounts. No centralised IAM for Linux.
Level 2 - Developing: Centralised auth partially deployed. More than 30% of servers still on local-only accounts.
Level 3 - Defined: Centralised auth on more than 70% of servers. Local accounts documented and minimised.
Level 4 - Managed: More than 95% of servers use centralised auth. Local accounts limited to break-glass only.
Level 5 - Optimized: 100% centralised auth. Break-glass accounts vaulted in PAM. Full joiners, movers, leavers integration.

Definition: % of scheduled uptime during which Linux servers are available and fully operational, excluding planned maintenance.
Level 1 - Ad Hoc: No uptime monitoring. Availability unknown. Outages discovered by users.
Level 2 - Developing: Basic ICMP monitoring. Approximately 95% availability. No SLA. Reactive incident management.
Level 3 - Defined: Agent-based monitoring via Nagios, Zabbix, or Prometheus. Availability tracked versus SLA. Targeting 99%.
Level 4 - Managed: 99.5% availability. Automated alerting and on-call integration. Capacity planning active.
Level 5 - Optimized: 99.9% or higher availability. Predictive monitoring. Automated failover. Proactive capacity management.

Definition: % of Linux servers synchronised to an authoritative NTP source, with time drift within acceptable thresholds of less than 1 second.
Level 1 - Ad Hoc: No NTP policy. Servers use default or no NTP. Time drift is common and unmonitored.
Level 2 - Developing: NTP configured on most servers but not monitored. Drift detected reactively.
Level 3 - Defined: NTP compliance tracked. More than 85% of servers within drift threshold. Alerts on failures.
Level 4 - Managed: More than 98% NTP compliance. Monitoring automated. Drift alerts trigger auto-remediation.
Level 5 - Optimized: 100% NTP compliance. Chrony or NTPsec enforced via configuration management. Zero drift incidents.

Definition: % of Linux servers managed via Infrastructure-as-Code or configuration management tools such as Ansible, Puppet, Chef, or Salt, ensuring consistent and auditable configuration.
Level 1 - Ad Hoc: All servers built and managed manually. No configuration management tooling.
Level 2 - Developing: Configuration management tools deployed but used inconsistently. Less than 40% of estate managed.
Level 3 - Defined: Between 40-75% of estate managed via IaC. Playbooks or modules for common tasks.
Level 4 - Managed: Between 75-95% managed via IaC. Drift detection integrated. Changes via code review pipeline.
Level 5 - Optimized: More than 95% managed via IaC. Immutable infrastructure model. GitOps workflow. Full audit trail.

Definition: % of Linux servers whose actual configuration deviates from the approved IaC-defined baseline at any given time.
Level 1 - Ad Hoc: No baseline defined. Configuration state is unknown.
Level 2 - Developing: Baseline documented but drift not measured. Manual periodic audits only.
Level 3 - Defined: Drift monitored on more than 70% of estate. Reports generated. Remediation is manual.
Level 4 - Managed: Drift detected automatically. Below 5% drift rate. Auto-remediation for approved deviations.
Level 5 - Optimized: Below 1% drift rate. Real-time detection. Auto-remediation within minutes. Full change audit log.

Definition: % of Linux servers forwarding system, application, and security logs to a centralised logging platform such as a SIEM, ELK stack, or Splunk.
Level 1 - Ad Hoc: No central log collection. Logs stored locally only. No visibility.
Level 2 - Developing: Less than 60% of servers forwarding logs. Coverage inconsistent. Log format not standardised.
Level 3 - Defined: Between 60-85% of servers centralised. Common log format adopted. Basic alerting in place.
Level 4 - Managed: More than 95% log centralisation. Log retention policy enforced. Alerting rules defined.
Level 5 - Optimized: 100% centralisation. Structured logging. Real-time correlation. SIEM fully integrated.

Definition: % of Linux servers included in a backup schedule, combined with frequency of successful recovery tests validating restore capability.
Level 1 - Ad Hoc: No backup policy for Linux servers. Data loss risk unmanaged.
Level 2 - Developing: Backups configured but not monitored. Recovery never tested. Less than 80% of servers covered.
Level 3 - Defined: Backup coverage above 85%. Success rate monitored. Recovery tested once per year.
Level 4 - Managed: Coverage above 98%. Backup success rate above 98%. Recovery tested quarterly. RTO and RPO defined.
Level 5 - Optimized: More than 99% coverage. Automated recovery validation. Immutable backups. RTO and RPO tested monthly.
